This is an interesting theory. It makes very logical sense to me. This also explains genetic per-disposition. Genetic altering of humans is a very delicate and morally sensitive subject. I think that to prevent cancer (and other diseases caused by genetic malfunction) it is our duty to prove its viability, but also to make sure it is only used in the most moral way possible. (I.E. lets not become Gattaca)

I've heard the argument before that cancer is effectively a higher life form evolving back into a single celled life form.

HeLa is a great example, since that strain has an entertaining habit of surviving all over the place and infecting other experiments in the same lab.

Except that evolution is ultimately about increasing an organism's probability of passing on genetic information.

Cancer fails as it kills its' host.

Bacteria, germs, viruses, and parasites that infect hosts without killing them, better yet without impacting their activity or even better still improving a host's functions are much, much more evolutionarily successful than those that simply kill off their host. As they either will not be as actively avoided if not encouraged to reproduce by their host species.

Look at smallpox or polio vs. chickenpox. The first two are eradicated, or headed there and the third is not. Mainly because it is not deadly or significantly debilitating.

It is valid for the cells: If cancer cells are more fit in a smokers body, they are more probable to survive and spread. You might call it micro-evolution. Nevertheless, it changes nothing about the outcome, though. So it won't change humanity's evolution, I guess.

Not quite. First of all, you're confusing natural selection with evolution. Natural selection is one mechanism that drives evolution, but the two aren't equivalent. I don't blame you for this; modern textbooks approach the subject in an incomplete fashion.

Second, your argument assumes that individual cells have some kind of an understanding of their relation to the organism, when really they operate in different levels of abstraction. A human exists in his or her environment and responds accordingly. A pulmonary cell exists inside the human body and reacts accordingly -- it lies on a more narrowly focused level of abstraction. Think of the example of mitochondria. They were likely an ancient prokaryote that, through the not yet understood processes of endosymbiosis, became a part of a eukaryote, or perhaps part of an organism straight away. This shows that cells are capable of looking out for themselves based on their specific environments, although in this case the result is a symbiotic relationship.

This is called metaplasia. After being exposed to nocive stimuli chronically, cells epxress different genes so they can transform into a more resistant type of cell.

The same happens with Barret's esophagus. People who have gastroesophageal reflux disease damage their esophagi with constant exposition to gastric acid. The cells transform to glandular cells (similar to the ones found in the small intestine) in order to survive. Of coruse, this is a precancerous transformation.

HA! New thinking my ass. This is a debate that goes all the way back to the great debate of germ theory between Louis Pasteur and Antoine Béchamp.

Pasteur argued that we should focus our medicine on fighting pathogens. Béchamp argued that the most important thing is ensuring that tissue remains healthy, thereby ensuring that pathogens can't take hold. On his deathbed, Pasteur recanted his position in favor of Béchamp's. By that point the damage was already done, the science was "settled" (sound familiar?), and we entered an era of focusing medicine entirely on mitigating the damage caused by pathogens. We have had wonderful advances, but also terrible setbacks. Antibiotics are the best example of the dual outcome. Antibiotics have saved countless lives from deadly infections, but at the expense of breeding increasingly frightening super bugs. Also consider vaccines. They have saved many, many lives, but long term use causes vaccine failure. Additionally, there just aren't that many vaccines in existence compared to the strains of diseases to which you can succumb.

I think both Pasteur and Béchamp were correct. Fighting pathogens is important and useful, but dangerous when we only focus on that side of the coin. Promoting healthy tissue is imperative as well. Perhaps it is even more essential. It appears that this same concept may apply to cancer, as this article explains. This is yet another illustration of science turning into an echo chamber, resulting in the complete disregard of a useful and valid idea for decades. In this case, since the 1860's.
